**Title:** Authoring dialogic identities in collaboration with artificial intelligence

**Authors:**  
Chris Proctor, University at Buffalo, State University of New York, [chrisp@buffalo.edu](mailto:chrisp@buffalo.edu), 0000-0003-3492-9590  
Varun Bhatt, University at Buffalo, State University of New York, [vbhatt2@buffalo.edu](mailto:vbhatt2@buffalo.edu), 0009-0009-2900-4367  
Ryan Rish, University at Buffalo, State University of New York, [ryanrish@buffalo.edu](mailto:ryanrish@buffalo.edu), 0000-0001-9751-3782

**Abstract:**  
As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday writing practices, the field of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) faces a foundational question: to what extent can interaction with large language models constitute collaboration, and what are the implications for authorship, identity, and agency? This article argues that a dialogic understanding of identity is essential for conceptualizing collaborative writing with AI. Drawing on theories of dialogism and identity from literacy studies, we conceptualize writing with AI as a negotiation among multiple voices in which authorial roles—animator, author, and principal—are distributed and reconfigured. We introduce new AI-supported writing affordances developed in Unfold Studio, a web application for reading and writing interactive stories, which enable writers to declaratively delegate elements of description, plot, and characterization to AI while retaining overall narrative control. Through contrasting case studies of two youth authors participating in an after-school writing club, we analyze how different dialogic authorial identities emerge in collaboration with AI—one marked by enthusiastic co-authorship and validation, and the other by resistance and critical distance. We discuss implications for understanding collaboration, identity, and criticality in AI-mediated literacy practices and outline directions for CSCL research in the age of generative AI.

**Keywords:** identity authorship, dialogic identity, collaborative writing, generative artificial intelligence, design-based research

# **Introduction**

As its name suggests, the field of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) tends to conceptualize computers as tools which mediate and support collaboration, but not as primary participants in collaboration. As generative artificial intelligence backed by large language models (hereafter discussed colloquially as AI) becomes ever more capable and is incorporated into more niches of our lives, a central question for the field is: to what extent can interaction with large language models constitute a form of collaboration? If we can collaborate with AI, what are the implications for human meaning-making and learning?   
CSCL has a long history of theorizing how technologies participate in learning and collaboration, including work on intelligent tutoring systems, distributed cognition, and restructuration. Today’s questions about the role of AI in education echo earlier debates about calculators in mathematics or programming in computer science: how much agency should be delegated to computational systems, and under what conditions does such delegation support learning? From this perspective, interactions with AI can be framed as collaborative, provided that human authors retain a shared understanding of the task and maintain responsibility for what is to be accomplished.  
However, collaboration with AI extends beyond task delegation and epistemic coordination. Unlike earlier educational technologies, AI systems capably participate in the same cultural discourses we use to anchor our identities, and are likely to influence both the texts we write as well as how authors understand themselves as writers and meaning-makers. CSCL has largely considered writing a medium for epistemic work; writing as a form of social action has been less considered.  
We argue that a dialogic understanding of identity provides a productive framework for conceptualizing collaborative writing with AI. Dialogism emphasizes that meaning emerges through interaction among multiple voices, each shaped by histories of prior use and anticipation of future audiences. From this perspective, writing is always already collaborative—not only among co-present authors, but also among genres, discourses, and imagined audiences.  
To explore these ideas empirically, we introduce new AI-supported writing affordances developed for Unfold Studio, a web application for reading and writing interactive stories. These affordances allow authors to declaratively delegate aspects of description, plot progression, and characterization to AI while retaining control over narrative structure and reader experience. We then analyze two contrasting case studies of youth authors using these interfaces, illustrating how different dialogic identities emerge in collaboration with AI.  
Our central research questions are: 

1. How is authorship distributed in collaborative writing with AI?   
2. How does the dialogic nature of authors’ identities shape the writing process? 

# **Background**

## **Writing as a collaborative project**

In this article, we are interested in writing as a form of social action in which meaning is co-produced by the author(s) of a text and its readers (Bazerman & Prior, 2004; Behizadeh, 2014; Dyson, 1993; 1997; Prior, 2006; Razafar & Gutierrez, 2003; Schultz & Fecho, 2000). The first tenant of this conceptualization is that all writing is social: no writer writes in a vacuum. Even when writing alone for oneself, there is an imagined other receiving and making sense of the text. The extent to which writing has shared meaning and significance for an identifiable group of people (e.g., students in a classroom, writers in a writing group, friends in a group chat) helps us understand these social acts of writing as constituting literacy practices, or social practices mediated by language use (Heath, 1983; Street, 1984). Literacy practices may be situated within particular contexts, such as school (Street & Street, 1991), and may be taken up across multiple contexts and social spaces (Leander & Sheehy, 2004). Although we understand textual meaning-making to be distributed across the participants of a literacy practice (such that authors and readers could be understood as asynchronously collaborating in meaning-making), our focus in this article is on synchronous collaboration during the composition of writing.  
This framing of writing, grounded in the field of literacy studies (Rowsell & Pahl, 2015), is uncommon in CSCL. Writing has been widely studied as a collaborative task in CSCL, but the emphasis is almost always on epistemology rather than on rhetoric or communication. For example, writing has been studied as a medium for improving ideas (e.g. Scardamalia and Bereiter, 2006), as a medium for creating shared meanings (e.g. Stahl, 2006), and as a venue for constructing knowledge through argumentation (e.g. Weinberger and Fischer, 2006), among others. We argue in the discussion (below) that a rhetorical and dialogic approach which asks, “Who is speaking here? Who is being addressed? Where does this language come from?” may be an important complement to epistemic approaches (“Is this true? How do I know?”) in supporting learners’ agency in the age of AI.   
Although our framing of writing is atypical for CSCL, it is an excellent task for collaboration, defined by Roschelle and Teasley (1995) as “a coordinated, synchronous activity that is the result of a continued attempt to construct and maintain a shared conception of a problem” (p. 70). In our framing of writing, the problem is to create an evocative text which has the potential to provoke certain experiences for readers. Our conceptualization of authorship is already distributed, drawing on genres and voices already present in the literacy practice and in implicit dialogue with the intended audience. This view of writing is not easily decomposable into subtasks, and therefore lends itself to collaboration as distinguished from cooperation: “In cooperation, partners split the work, solve sub-tasks individually and then assemble the partial results into the final output. In collaboration, partners do the work ‘together’” (Dillenbourg, 1999, p. 8). When multiple people collaborate on this kind of writing, they are likely to make these latent influences explicit.   
As we explore the prospect of collaborative writing with AI, we will distinguish three authorial roles which are typically collapsed within that term: *animator, author,* and *principal* (Goffman, 1981; Goff & Rish, 2020). The *animator* is the person who actually inscribes the word on the page or screen, the *author* is the person who selects the sentiments and ideas, and the *principal* is the person “who is committed to what the words say” (Goffman, 1981, p. 144). These authorial roles can illuminate why we have readily come to accept AI in some social contexts but reject it in others. For example, AI has been rapidly adopted in composing emails and text messages because there is a presumption that AI is helping its author find the words for what they already meant to say, just as a greeting card may feel sincere even though it has a pre-printed message. The email’s sender delegates the role of animator to AI, but retains the roles of author (setting the intent of the message) and principal (if you send the email, you are accountable for its contents). There have been several high-profile scandals in which university administrators or government leaders publish heartfelt emotional responses to tragedies, which are later revealed to have been composed with AI. The weight of the message comes from the leader’s claimed personal reaction; the fraudulent author role provokes a sense of betrayal. Finally, AI tends to be extremely controversial when it presumes an ersatz role of principal, such as chatbots for romantic companionship. How can intersubjectivity, promises, or commitments have significance when there is nobody on the other end of the line? 

## **Dialogic identity**

Dialogism is the epistemological view that meaning is constituted through ongoing interaction among multiple voices, rather than being grounded in individual cognition and fixed textual meanings (Bakhtin, 1981). A dialogic understanding of writing and literacy recognizes that meaning is co-produced by authors, readers, and context. The words we use have histories  and we take them up to form new assemblages that are related to these prior uses and also in anticipation of how our readers will take them up for their own future use. Schultz and Fecho (2000) argue that “the word is embedded in a context of individual and societal importance. Language becomes one’s own only when expropriated from others” (p. 53). The process of figuring out who we are and how we are going to act involves a constant back-and-forth with our social and cultural context. AI models language, but it also models culture and discourse, so when we interact with AI our identities and agency are likely to become intertwined.  
CSCL has substantial existing engagement with dialogism (Stahl, Cress, Ludvigsen, & Law, 2014), including the epistemic stance that distributed meaning-making through argumentation and writing, as a design goal (Fischer, Killar, Stegmann, Wecker, & Zottman, 2013), and informing methodological approaches (Koschmann, 1996). However, in line with our claim (above) that CSCL focuses on writing as an epistemic medium rather than as rhetoric or social action, CSCL tends to focus on how knowledge and meaning are produced dialogically rather than on how dialogism shapes who we can be (identity) and what we can do (agency) as speakers and authors. 

Theories of identity in the learning sciences often work within Vygotsky’s (1980) paradigm of learning as internalization of social practices. Sfard & Prusak (2005) define identity as “reifying, significant, endorsable stories about a person,” emphasizing that identities are not expressed in stories, but are themselves stories (p. 14). They argue for identity as a more useful analytic construct than learning precisely because it functions as an interface. They critique constructs such as beliefs and attitudes as presuming a stable inner version of a person which a particular analysis might or might not accurately describe. They make a related critique of treating narrative as evidence of identity, because this framing again presumes an authentic but inaccessible version of self. We recognize that identities can be durable and develop over time (e.g. Sfard & Prusak’s (2005) designated identities which develop over time, Gee’s (2001) identity trajectories, or Markus and Nurius’s (1986) possible selves), but in this article, we are focused on shorter-term and locally-situated authorship of identity. Our focus on shorter time-frames and specific situated contexts was partly forced by considerations of what is feasible to research, but also by our sense that identity really is an ever-shifting performance which, when it is stable over time, is more attributable to stability of context and practices of self-narration than about the accretion of a durable character (Mishler, 2004).  
The primary theoretical contribution of this article is the argument that a dialogic understanding of identity and agency (based primarily in the work of Holland, Lachicotte, Skinner, and Cain (1998)) is essential for conceptualizing collaboration with AI systems. We understand identity as a model of selfhood one authors and occupies within in a literacy practice, which exists at the interface “between intimate discourses, inner speaking, and bodily practices formed in the past and the discourses and practices to which people are exposed, willingly or not, in the present” (Holland et al., 1998, p. 32). Identity is dialogic and constantly re-negotiated in context: “An identity depends on the individual’s understanding (or lack of understanding) of how that identity will be recognized in that relationship, time, or context. The person is called into an identity by the recognitions or assignments of others, and the meanings the person makes of the identities available to him or her serve to constitute a sense of self or subjectivity” (Moje & Luke, 2009, p. 419). Identity authorship means crafting who you are and will be in a literacy practice, staking out what kinds of action may be possible (having or gaining author-ity) but where power is also exercised through the shaping and maintenance of subject positions (being author-ized). 

# **New interfaces for collaborative writing with AI**

Drawing on the theoretical framework developed in the previous section, we developed a high-level conjecture (Sandoval, 2014\) that *dialogic identity is important for collaborating with AI and for understanding such collaboration.* As part of an ongoing design-based research project exploring this conjecture, we have designed and implemented new interfaces for AI-supported writing as extensions to Unfold Studio (Authors, 2019), a web-based platform for reading and writing interactive stories. Stories in Unfold Studio are written in a programming language called Ink (Inkle, 2019\) which offers familiar features of programming languages such as variables and control structures, while giving primacy to text, not code. When a reader plays a story, they are presented with text and then are presented with choices. The reader makes a choice, and then sees more text and choices in a cycle which continues until the story ends. Each of the interfaces (described in detail below) is implemented as a built-in function which can be called during the execution flow of a story to generate text. When these functions are invoked during story runs, they make calls to Unfold Studio’s server, which calls a generative AI service and does additional processing before returning the generated response. The reader does not interact with these functions directly, and generated text is not marked as such in a story run–although a story’s source code is always available to readers, and we often observe readers reading the source at the same time as they are playing through a story.   
We call this form of story-writing *declarative narrative*: just as declarative programming is a paradigm in which the author expresses an intent and the computer figures out the details, the author of a declarative narrative delegates components of the text to generative AI, while retaining overall control of the text. The three functions described below, *generate*, *continue*, and *agent*, provide affordances for delegating sensory detail, plot, and characterization respectively. Unfold Studio stories can import components from other stories, making it possible to modularize and recombine literary elements from other stories. Figure 1 shows the source code for a student-authored story which uses the generate and continue functions. A play-through of the story is shown in Figure 2; each of the new interfaces is then explained with reference to Figures 1 and 2\.

**Figure 2\.** Text of a story play-through generated from the source code in Figure 1\. 

The generate function generates text in response to a provided prompt. This interface is similar in function to generative AI interfaces such as ChatGPT, although in this context, control flow returns to the story after the generated text.   
If the generate function involves delegating details to AI, the continue function involves delegating components of the plot. The continue function prompts the story to automatically generate a series of talk turns: open-ended user input followed by a response. The continue function requires one argument, the target knot where the story will resume. The responses within the series of talk turns guide the story toward this knot; at each turn, the continue function evaluates the user’s input and the generative AI decides whether it is a plausible continuation of the story heading toward the target knot; if not, the user input is rejected. When the user’s input is sufficiently close to the content of the target according to the generativa AI, the story resumes with the content of the target knot. If the target story knot contains multiple options (not shown here), then the generative AI will guide the story toward whichever option is assessed to be most reachable, allowing the open-ended interaction to resume the scripted story at one of multiple re-entry points.   
Finally, the agent function can be used to delegate characters to GAI. The agent function requires two arguments, target and character, both knots in the story. The target function plays the same role as the  continue function: agent takes control of the story’s execution flow until the AI system determines that the story can continue at target. Before generating responses, however, the agent plays through the character as a sub-story and uses it to create a model of a character. The responses generated by the agent are in the voice of this character. The character sub-story can take many forms, for example an interview, a compilation of facts about a historical person, or a rambling stream-of-consciousness narrative.  
We believe these AI extensions to interactive storytelling are promising for supporting and understanding dialogic identity authorship–a hunch which is borne out in the case studies presented below. The three affordances loosely correspond to delegation of the three authorial roles introduced in the previous section. The generate function delegates the role of animator by expressing authorial intent via the prompt. The continue function additionally delegates the role of author (allowing the AI system to decide what will happen through negotiation with the player), while retaining the principal role by bounding the continue function at an explicitly-defined starting point and ending point within the larger story. Finally, the agent function potentially introduces a co-principal to the story. It would be possible to write a story which enacts a dynamic struggle for control between the authorial voice and the story’s characters.   
These affordances make visible dynamics which already exist in prose in more subtle forms–a potential benefit for pedagogical applications. The explicit scripting of interaction between the author’s words and the reader’s choices is a concrete instantiation of dialogic meaning-making (Authors, 2020), similar to Graff and Birkenstein’s (2006)  “They say, I say” framework for making multivocality explicit when teaching academic writing. Interactive stories can be nonlinear (there may be more paths through the story than can be explored in one playthrough) and nondeterministic (using randomness or prompts to AI affordances which include user input), making visible Rosenblatt’s (1968) argument that a text is recreated on every reading. And the ability to delegate specific elements of the text to AI while retaining the overall role of author makes it possible to position the AI-generated voices in specific relationships to the reader’s in-story identity. 

# **Methods**

## **Context**

This study took place during ten weeks of an after-school writing club at a high school in a small city in the northeast of the United States, led by the first author. The curriculum was structured as a writer’s workshop (Dorn & Soffos, 2001\) in which students spend most of their time writing personally-meaningful stories, sharing their writing with peers, and participating in optional mini-lessons focused on specific aspects of writing craft. Following Authors (2019), mini-lessons were used to introduce the computational and AI affordances described above via simple story templates, with an emphasis on the rhetorical possibilities of these affordances rather than on using them according to an a priori idea of correctness. As the weeks progressed, participants shifted from practicing techniques with quick, short stories to working on more substantial stories over a longer period of time, culminating with one final story shared with the club at the last meeting. In a previous analysis (Authors, in submission), we discuss the design of the AI affordances in more detail and compare the corpus of stories using AI affordances with a comparable corpus written before AI affordances were introduced. The story structure and developmental trajectory of  AI and non-AI stories were broadly similar. 

## **Data sources**

This article deals with four sources of data: the sequence of story versions saved as authors develop a story, records of authors’ playthroughs of their stories, the first author’s fieldnotes from the writing club, including ongoing discussions with the focal students about their authorial intentions and experiences writing in collaboration with AI, and pre- and post-surveys about participants’ prior AI use, experiences with using AI in Unfold Studio, and their writing identities.   
Every time an author saves a story or re-plays a story after making edits (implicitly saving), the story is recompiled and a version is saved. Using the methods developed in Authors (2019), each adjacent pair of story versions can be compared, and the differences between the versions can be classified. Therefore, a story with n versions yields a sequence of n-1 story edits, each classified into one of the following categories:

* **Debugging**: The edit results in a story which fails to compile.  
* **AI**: The edit adds or changes a line containing one of the AI affordances.   
* **Code**: The edit adds or changes a line which affects the computational structure of the story, such as changing how parts of the story are linked together, presenting options to the reader, manipulating a variable, or calling a function.   
* **Text**: The edit adds or changes story text, without changing the structure of the story. 

Unfold Studio also logs every playthrough of a story, recording the choices readers make when presented with options, open-ended input readers provide when prompted with a text box or during an AI-guided invocation of continue, and the text which is generated by invocations of the AI affordances. In this article, we focus on authors’ playthroughs of their own stories during the writing process. 

## **Analysis of case studies**

This article analyzes how two focal authors developed stories with Unfold Studio’s AI affordances, offering contrasting cases of dialogic authorial identity. The analytical approach is a kind of literary analysis developed by Authors (2019), focusing on how authors use familiar literary elements such as character, plot, and irony as well as new affordances such as variables, randomness, and AI, for rhetorical effect and potential reader experience. Our primary evidence is authors’ story edits and playthroughs; Figures 3 and 4 plot the development of focal students’ stories, showing the sequence of each class of story edits and story playthroughs over time. Note that while these plots show the sequence of different classes of story edits, they do not show the magnitude of changes: changing a single word or adding several paragraphs at once both appear as a single text edit. We use conversations with authors recorded in fieldnotes (and occasionally survey results) for context and to ground claims about authorial intent. We focus on collaboration between the human authors and the AI by analyzing how they inhabit the three authorial roles described above (animator, author, and principal). 

# **Case 1: Dragonbaby**

Dragonbaby is a girl in ninth grade who attended the writing club and collaborated continuously with her sister, who is in twelfth grade. The two sisters used the same Unfold Studio account in the style of pair-programming (so we cannot distinguish their contributions); Dragonbaby was typing during almost all the club meetings. Both sisters are avid readers of fantasy novels and enjoy writing in the fan-fiction genre. Dragonbaby’s final story, “Our actions have consequences,” is a fan-fiction story set in the world of *Percy Jackson & the Olympians* (Riordan, 2006), a series of novels which juxtaposes the world of the Olympian gods with today’s world. We chose to include another story, “Worlds collide” (which imagines characters from Percy Jackson crossing into the world of Hogwarts from Harry Potter) in our analysis because Dragonbaby worked on this story at the same time using it as a scratch pad to test ideas and techniques which were then used in “Our actions have consequences.”   
![][image1]  
**Figure 3\.** Combined history of Dragonbaby’s two stories,   
“Our actions have consequences” and “Worlds collide.” 

Several features are immediately visible in the story history shown in Figure 3: There is an intense period of debugging at the beginning paired with a burst of code edits as Dragonbaby learned to work with the programming language. Then, starting April 27, there is a period of intense text and code edits with less and less debugging, as Dragonbaby developed the structure of the story. AI affordances are added in the last half of story development, after most of the text and code was in place. Dragonbaby did not actually play though the story until AI edits were introduced on May 8 (for a linear story, it is easy enough to read the source code as the text of the story), but the addition of AI affordances kicked off an intense period of playing the story (usually testing the effect of passing different prompts to the generate function, either as user input during a playthrough or by editing hard-coded prompts (which appear as AI edits). By the end of the workshop, Dragonbaby was no longer editing the story at all, instead repeatedly playing through it. Dragonbaby continued playing the story in the weeks after the workshop ended.  
As Dragonbaby and her sister experimented with integrating AI-generated text into her story, they were delighted to discover that the large language model powering Unfold Studio’s AI features (currently OpenAI’s gpt-4o model) was aware of the content of the novels, and that they could produce descriptions of settings and characters from the book using generate, and could interact with the book’s plot using continue. Their experience may have been heightened by novelty: that neither had used generative AI before.

| :---- | :---- |

In terms of authorial roles, Dragonbaby frequently delegated the animator role to AI through multiple calls to *generate* and *continue* providing text to the reader, while retaining a clear authorial intent. For example, Table 1 shows four versions of the prompt passed to the generate function; these versions are interspersed with story plays in which Dragonbaby examines the generated text before tweaking the prompt again. The final version of the prompt adds Danielle Malfoy, explicitly anchoring that character to the world of Harry Potter.   
	Dragonbaby and her sister increasingly shared authorship roles with AI as well. They were delighted to discover that the LLM was able to generate narratives corresponding to the Percy Jackson universe (implying that the Percy Jackson novels were included in the training data). For example, in one part of the story the character boards a ship named the Princess Andromeda and then the reader is prompted to decide what she wants to do, which is stored in a variable called what\_to\_do. This input is injected into a prompt to generate: "You are the narrator of what happens once Luke has told you that you are on the Princess Andromeda ship from Percy Jackson Sea of Monsters. The player wants to do this: " \+ what\_to\_do \+ ". Narrate the next step in a story where they succeed. Without speaking of an explosian." Here, the AI takes on a co-authorial role, dynamically deciding what will happen next with some guidance from Dragonbaby.   
Although Dragonbaby clearly retained the role of principal, proudly referring to it as her story and sharing it with everyone who was willing to read it, and Dragonbaby strongly agreed with survey questions such as “As an author, it is important for me to have my own writing voice” and “I have my own identity as a writer.” However, she also began to regard the AI as taking on a subtle principal role. Through her intensive replaying of the story, exploring and coaxing generative text from the AI, Dragonbaby and her sister discovered that the AI could reproduce the lore of the Percy Jackson and Harry Potter worlds, and they began to geek out (Horst, Herr-Stephenson, & Robinson, 2010\) together in a fan-fiction literacy practice. These stories were important identity texts (Paris, 2011\) for Dragonbaby and her sister; the AI’s ability to respond and interact with the stories catalyzed the development of positive dialogic identities embedded in the AI-generated discourse. 

# **Case 2: Quaezae** 

Quaezae is a girl in tenth-grade, fairly quiet and preferring to work alone in the writing club. Although Quaezae had never done any programming before, she was very interested in the computational aspects of interactive stories and developed a complex story using multiple variables to create a shopping simulation which concludes with the cashier ringing up all the purchases and summing the total bill. When the GAI affordances were introduced, Quaezae expressed moral opposition to using GAI as well as fear of its possible effects on her, telling the workshop facilitator (the first author) that she felt GAI was ruining her friends’ minds. She admitted to occasionally using GAI, but only on her friends’ phones so that it would not be connected with her. At first, she was opposed to participating in the workshop at all, but after discussing how the technology worked with the facilitator, and being invited to experiment with GAI to become better-informed in her opposition, she decided to write “Tellers,” a dystopian story in which implanted AI chips are required to participate in society, and which are accepted as normal without complaint.  
![][image2]  
**Figure 4\.** History of Quaezae’s story, “Tellers.”

The development of “Tellers,” shown in Figure 4, is less extensive than Dragonbaby’s stories, with most of the edits taking place on a single day. Quaezae started by pasting in a previously-used story template which included a use of the generate function (because this was the first version of the story, it does not appear in Figure 4 as an AI edit) and testing its functionality with several playthroughs. In contrast to her earlier shopping story, Quaezae decided not to implement much computational complexity into “Tellers;” the debugging mostly involves her attempts to use a variable to record the player’s name, and then to inject the name into prompts to generate, producing dynamic text which addresses the player. As with Dragonbaby, Quaezae spent the final phase repeatedly playing through her story.   
In terms of authorship roles, Quaezae delegated the role of animator to AI through calls to generate, but did not share the author role with AI. Whereas Dragonbaby shared authorship by geeking out with AI on fan fiction, Quaezae’s engagement with AI was wary and reluctant. As discussed above, Quaezae was very cautious about providing any information that could identify her or connect her with AI, never even typing in a name when she played through her own story.   
“Tellers” is thematically concerned with the nonconsensual dialogic nature of AI, laid out explicitly in an epigraph which opens the story: “AI has completely been enthralled into our lives, most of us cant go an hour without a friend, family memeber of yourself coming across or using AI. In this world, its been complete accepted, or more accureately ... integrated.” The sense that AI has been “integrated” but not “accepted” is a perfect articulation of the dialogic nature of AI. Whereas Dragonbaby enjoyed authoring an identity entangled with AI through joint participation in a fan fiction literacy practice, Quaezae described fearing and resenting how AI is becoming part of us whether we like it or not.   
These concerns are reflected in the plot of “Tellers:” you go to a bank and are confronted by a teller who says you cannot access your account unless you consent to having an AI chip implanted in your arm. After several intermediary choices, the story has two endings, depending on whether you decide to have the chip implanted. If you choose the implant, the story ends with “Welcome back, Eric—how does it feel to be more than human? \[...\] As you go on with your life, you notice how…simple it is to have the new implant in your arm, your banking, checking and savings is all at your fingertips (or an arms reach- haha\!).” This ending is sarcastically glossed as “The Good Ending.” If you choose to “Reject modernity\!” the story ends with “You go on with your life like normal, living, breathing, still no implants…but less and less places accept your physical card, not to mention cash. You begin going down a path of stealing and crime, nothing abnormal to the city,” which is glossed as the “Neutral Ending.” For a reader of “Tellers,” the choice is between giving yourself up to AI or a failed life of social exclusion and crime. This is an example of interactional positioning (Wortham, 2000), a phenomenon in which positioning of a text’s in-story identities becomes reified in analogous positioning amongst the readers. The sarcastic tone feels appropriate to a story which only includes the GAI voice in order to reject it, perhaps also voicing a protest against pressure Quaezae felt from the facilitator to use AI in her writing.   
Quaezae asks the reader for your name at beginning of the story and then repeatedly injects your name into prompts to produce dynamically-generated content which addresses you by name. For the reader, this produces an unsettling experience of being unexpectedly put into dialogue with the story;in a real sense you are also put into dialogue with AI as well. If Quaezae retains the authorial role in “Tellers,” the voice of AI is present in the story in a way which suggests some distribution of the principal role in an adversarial mode. This is Quaezae’s story, but it is also AI’s story to some extent.  In “Tellers,” Quaezae reveals an authorial identity which is also dialogically enmeshed with AI, but against her will. The story feels claustrophobic, with the authorial voice rejecting something which she recognizes as part of herself. 

# **Discussion**

The key theoretical contribution of this article is that a dialogic account of identity is essential for conceptualizing and understanding collaboration with generative AI systems. Dragonbaby and Quaezae both recognize the dialogic nature of writing in collaboration with AI and both author identities which are distributed in literacy practices shaped by AI, but where Dragonbaby is inspired and validated by geeking out with AI, Quaezae is creeped out and “enthralled.” We believe similar dynamics are likely to emerge beyond the specific niche of interactive storytelling. AI-based media is better understood as an active collaborator in meaning-making than as a tool passively mediating collaboration between people. Instead of gaining control over AI as we internalize it (as with mediating tools), we co-author our identities and co-produce meanings with AI.   
If collaboration is about more than getting the job done–it is an encounter with others which may transform us and our understanding of the work–then collaboration with AI has the potential for a sinister sort of vulnerability without reciprocity. AI systems are trained on vast corpora and can participate powerfully in myriad literacy practices, but the motivations and biases encoded in AI are opaque and are shaped by commercial and geopolitical interests. Therefore, there is a need for dialogic criticality–not just an interrogation of AI as an external entity (for example, a pedagogy of algorithmic auditing (Morales-Navarro, et al., 2025)), but also a sort of introspection reflecting on our own authorial identities which are becoming fundamentally intertwined with AI.   
Interactive storytelling has particular potency for supporting criticality in youths’ digital worlds as a tool for dialogizing AI while remaining in control of the interpretive context. Bhaktin (1981) analyzes how novels destabilize other literary forms, so that they “become dialogized, permeated with laughter, irony, humor, elements of self-parody and finally… an indeterminacy, a certain semantic openendedness, a living contact with unfinished, still-evolving contemporary reality (the openended present).” (p. 7\) The novel can do this for the genres of print literacy: “Take, for example, the parodic sonnets with which Don Quixote begins. Although they are impeccably structured as sonnets, we could never possibly assign them to the sonnet genre. In Don Quixote they appear as part of a novel–but even the isolated parodic sonnet (outside the novel) could not be classified generically as a sonnet. In a parodied sonnet, the sonnet form is not a genre at all; that is, it is not the form of a whole but is rather the object of representation.” (p. 51\) One aim of Unfold Studio is to support a corresponding ability to write stories about AI-powered digital media. 

# **Conclusion**

Just as social media dialogized, colonized, and transformed our social relationships, AI is becoming ubiquitous in our literacy media and stands to dialogize our authorial identities–our understandings of who we are and what we can do. We are in the same situation as the reader in “Tellers;” opting in means being transformed in ways we cannot choose, but opting out may mean exclusion from important domains of social, political, and economic life. A dialogic understanding of identity can help bring into focus the mechanisms and consequences of our relationships with AI. The future is unclear, but we hope that technologies and pedagogies such as those explored in this article help create ways of being and critical possibilities for living in the age of AI.
